articles.title: Nudists, peaceniks and freeloading travellers: the people keeping the Esperanto dream alive
articles.summary: 世界语没有失败，是「最后胜利」死了：它活成了一种自愿的流散亚文化。
articles.briefing:
The usual obituary for Esperanto is that it failed. A Warsaw oculist invented a language so that strangers would stop killing one another; the League of Nations did not adopt it; English won; the file is closed. The Guardian long read — first published in Harper's — refuses the obituary. The claim is not that Zamenhof's project succeeded on its own terms. It is that the terms changed, and that what remains is not a corpse. Raŭmismo won. Finvenkismo, the doctrine of final victory, the dream that Esperanto would become the world's second language, has been mostly abandoned by the people who still speak it. What they kept is a chosen diaspora: a subculture that behaves like an ethnicity you can join, with its own beds, its own congresses, its own jokes about nudists and peaceniks and travellers who never pay for a room.

Pasporta Servo is the institution that makes the argument walk. You learn the language and you may sleep on the sofas of strangers who have agreed, in advance, that a shared invented grammar is enough of a kinship. Cheap travel replaced the bid for the League. Joy replaced the manifesto. Hobby clubs, naturist gatherings, meetings in cities that do not otherwise care: these are not consolation prizes in the piece. They are the form the language now takes. A world tongue that failed to become universal can still be a passport. The people keeping the dream alive are not waiting for ministries of education. They are hosting. The mockery in the headline — nudists, peaceniks, freeloaders — is the piece's own bait. Take it and you will miss the point. The ridicule is what a universalist project looks like after it has given up on the state and kept the house.

That would be a tidy irony if the old interna ideo were simply dead. It is not. The article travels to Congo, where pacifists still treat the language as a tool against the next war, and to Brno, where a Chinese priest says mass in it. Those scenes are not kitsch. They are the remainder of Zamenhof's moral bet: that a neutral tongue could make a guest of the stranger rather than an enemy. The naturists and the sofa-surfers are easy to laugh at. The mass is harder. So is the Congolese club. The long read's discipline is to hold both without deciding that one is the real Esperanto and the other a degeneration. A language can be a hobby and a creed in the same week. The people who still speak it have stopped pretending those uses must cancel each other.

A reader who has sat through the history of failed internationalisms will recognise the pattern. The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries were full of men who thought a grammar could do the work of a treaty. English did that work instead, badly, as an imperial leftover. Esperanto's surviving speakers are interesting because they stopped competing. They became a people. Diaspora is the right word only if you accept that a diaspora can be elective. Nobody is born an Esperantist. You choose to be a guest in a language that belongs to no state, and then you discover that the language has a state of mind: hospitality as ideology, travel as liturgy. The final victory was a League fantasy. The spare room is a practice.

This issue is titled 客人, guests. The Odyssey briefing that follows will talk about xenia, the law of receiving the stranger. Esperanto is the modern, slightly absurd, version of the same law. You do not have to believe that a Warsaw doctor can abolish war. You do have to notice that a network of spare rooms has outlived the League, and that a priest in Brno and a pacifist in Congo still think the old idea is worth a morning. Read the Guardian when you have a sitting. The original is where the nudists and the mass have to share a paragraph. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: Esperanto did not fail. The final victory failed. What remains is a people who decided that being each other's guests was enough.

articles.title: The Odyssey Wars
articles.summary: 艾哈迈德写诺兰的《奥德赛》：争的不是谁能穿青铜甲，是款待陌生人还算不算宙斯的法。
articles.briefing:
Ahmad's New Lines essay is not a review of costumes. Christopher Nolan's Odyssey, in his telling, is a film about a world in which the rules have already collapsed and might makes right — and about the one rule that is supposed to survive that collapse. Xenia: hospitality to the stranger. Homer's word, Zeus's law, the golden rule before the golden rule had a Sunday-school name. Nolan, Ahmad says, pivots the epic on that law. The suitors are not merely rude. They have broken the house. Odysseus's homecoming is not a Spartan-helmet fantasy. It is what happens when the guest-law fails and the host has to become a judge. A cinema culture that has spent a decade selling antiquity as abs and recruitment will hear this as a spoiler. It is a repossession.

The culture war around the film is the piece's other subject, and Ahmad will not let either side have the poem. The right attacks the casting: who is allowed to wear the bronze, who looks like a Greek, who has been let into a story that some viewers still treat as a bloodline. The left, with Emily Wilson named as the voice that finds the film didactic, attacks it for teaching. Both attacks, in Ahmad's account, miss what Nolan is doing with Homer. He is reclaiming the poem from chauvinists who have marched it into stadiums and posters. The Odyssey is not a manual for the strong. It is a manual for what the strong owe the person who arrives at the door. Didacticism is a charge that only works if you think Homer was entertainment without a law. He was not. The poem is a long argument about houses, guests, and the price of forgetting either.

The comparative move is the one that will stay with a reader who has any interest in hospitality as politics. Ahmad says Pashtun and Chitrali diyafa is closer to Homeric xenia than any reconstruction of a hoplite parade. The stranger is fed before he is questioned. The house is a temporary asylum. That is not a soft ethic. It is a hard one, because it binds the host when the host would rather be a king. A film that remembers this is doing something the helmet-and-abs version of antiquity cannot do. It is putting Zeus back in the guest room. For a Chinese reader who has been sold both the Western canon as prestige and the Western canon as propaganda, the cut is useful. The question is not whether Homer belongs to Europe. It is which Homer is being screened: the march, or the law of the door.

Dakhla is the blemish Ahmad will not sand off. Filming in Western Sahara, on land whose political status is not a period detail, is a real stain on a project that wants to talk about the ethics of arrival. The piece does not treat the location as a cancelled tweet. It treats it as a contradiction: you cannot preach xenia and treat a disputed territory as a backdrop. The argument is stronger for the admission. Nolan is not being crowned. He is being read. A digest that dropped Dakhla to keep the essay tidy would be doing the thing the piece refuses.

This issue keeps asking who counts as a guest. Esperanto built a sofa network out of an invented grammar. Higgins, next, will sit in a language classroom in a country under siege. Ahmad's Homer is the oldest version of the same question. Read New Lines. The original is where the casting fight and the Chitrali house have to sit in the same essay. This briefing is here so you know what you are opening: not a movie recap, and not a culture-war scorecard. A claim about which antiquity we are being sold, and which one we might still need when the rules have already gone.

articles.title: ‘The war leaked into every lesson’: learning Ukrainian in a country under siege
articles.summary: 希金斯在伊万诺-弗兰科夫斯克跟奥尔哈学乌克兰语：战争渗进每一课，字母本身就是抵抗。
articles.briefing:
Charlotte Higgins did not go to Ivano-Frankivsk for a tourist kit. She went to learn Ukrainian with Olha, and the Guardian long read is the record of what happens when a language class cannot pretend the street is elsewhere. The war leaked into every lesson: the title is not a metaphor she added later. It is the syllabus. Grammar examples are Zaluzhnyi, Zelenskyy, Putin. Verbs of motion, which in a peaceful classroom are a chore about going and coming, become a map of who left, who returned, who cannot. Tryvoha means the air-raid alarm and it means anxiety. You cannot learn the word without learning both. A student who wanted a clean vocabulary list will be disappointed. A student who wanted to know what a language is for in a country under siege will not.

The letters are the basic material, and Higgins treats them as such. Nathan Coley's work is in the piece because a letter is not only a sound. Ї becomes defiance in occupied Mariupol: a character the occupier would rather not see on a sign. Ґ, restored after Stalin, is a restitution you can write with a pen. These are not decorative facts for a feature on "the beauty of Ukrainian." They are the argument. A language that has been reduced, renamed, and punished does not arrive as a neutral tool. It arrives as a decision. To learn it in Ivano-Frankivsk, while the war is on, is to accept that the classroom is already a political room. Olha is not a tour guide. She is a teacher whose examples cannot be fictionalised into Ivan and Maria going to the shop.

Learning, Higgins insists, is vulnerability. You mispronounce. You forget the motion verb. You sit in someone else's grammar while the city practices the other tryvoha. The piece will not let you convert that vulnerability into a sentimental story about a Western journalist finding herself. The finding is smaller and harder: you are a guest in a language that is being fought over, and the host is not obliged to make you comfortable. The war is not background colour. It is the reason the lesson exists in this form. A digest that filed this under "culture" is not aestheticising the war. It is saying that culture, here, is the thing that occupies the same hour as the siren.

This issue's other culture pieces are about invented hospitality and Homeric hospitality. Higgins is about linguistic hospitality of a harsher kind. Esperanto offers a sofa if you learn the grammar. Homer's xenia feeds the stranger before asking his name. Ukrainian, in this classroom, asks you to take on a history before you can order coffee. The three pieces belong together because they refuse the idea that a language is a kit. Zamenhof wanted a kit that would abolish war. Olha is teaching a language that war has already entered. Nolan, in Ahmad's reading, wants Zeus's law back. Higgins wants you to feel the weight of a single character on a wall in Mariupol. Coley's letter-as-material is the art-world name for what Mariupol already knew: a character on a wall is not decoration. It is a claim about who is allowed to live in the script.

Read the Guardian when you have a sitting. The long read is where the motion verbs and the siren have to share a page, and where Coley's sense of the letter as material stops being an art-world aside. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: you are not learning Ukrainian as a hobbyist collecting fronts. You are sitting in a country that has made the alphabet a front, and the only honest way to be a guest there is to let the war into the lesson.

articles.title: Iraq’s impossible predicament: why the country is trapped between Iran and the US
articles.summary: 阿卜杜勒-阿哈德写伊拉克：哈梅内伊死后平衡破裂，国家靠两个敌人活着。
articles.briefing:
Ghaith Abdul-Ahad's long read is not a primer on Iraqi factions. It is an argument that the country's famous balancing act was always a dependence, and that the dependence became visible the moment the balance collapsed. After Khamenei's killing, Iraq could no longer pretend to be the clever guest of two patrons. Iran-backed IRI militias attacked Iraqi oil; Basra's output fell by two-thirds. The American-backed prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, ordered disarmament by 30 September. Oil revenues sit at the New York Fed. The United States stopped dollar shipments and then resumed them. The sequence is not a newsreel. It is a mechanism. One host can starve the house. The other can set fire to the garden. The guest has to thank both.

The old man on the Basra corniche is the sentence the piece needs and will not decorate. We must support Iran; America will not let the economy collapse. That is not a theory of alignment. It is a theory of insurance. You pay the nearer militia in loyalty because the farther treasury still clears the cheques. A state whose oil money lives in New York and whose armed groups answer, in part, to Tehran is not non-aligned. It is doubly aligned, which is another word for trapped. Abdul-Ahad has spent years walking this beat. The value of the piece is that he will not let the predicament be moralised into a choice Iraq has simply refused to make. The choice is the predicament. There is no third patron waiting in the Gulf with a clean cheque and no invoice.

Disarmament by a date certain is the kind of sentence that reads well in a capital. In Basra it reads as a dare. Militias that have just hit the oil that pays the state are being told to become a memory by the end of September. The United States, having demonstrated that it can turn the dollar tap, has demonstrated that it can also turn it back on. That is not reassurance. It is a reminder of who owns the plumbing. Iran, having lost Khamenei, has not lost the groups that can still make Iraqi export numbers fall off a cliff. The two-thirds drop is the number to keep. It is the price of being the corridor between two enemies who have stopped pretending the corridor is neutral.

This issue's title is guests. Iraq is the dark version. Esperanto's guests chose their hosts. Homer's guests were sacred. Higgins is a guest in a language under siege. Iraq is a guest in a financial and military house it does not own. The corniche line will travel because it is shameless and accurate. A university reader who has been trained to sort the region into axes and proxies should feel the piece as a correction. The axis is the trap. The proxy is the country. Dollar shipments that stop and then resume are not a subplot about liquidity. They are the same lesson as the two-thirds drop in Basra: one patron withholds the blood, the other spills it, and the state writes both down as weather. Zaidi's September date and the Fed account belong in one sentence. A deadline without a treasury is theatre. A treasury without a monopoly on force is a hostage note. Abdul-Ahad's patience is the refusal to pick a cleaner story.

Read the Guardian. The original is where the Fed account and the Basra walk have to sit in the same essay, and where Abdul-Ahad's patience with Iraqi contradiction is the method, not the mood. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: after the balancing act died, what remained was a state that must support one enemy so the other will keep it alive.

articles.title: A bungled bomb plot in Poland exposed a spy – but whose spy was he?
articles.summary: 罗戈夫既是FSB线人也是乌克兰的笨信使；流亡圈要的不是超级间谍，是互相怀疑。
articles.briefing:
Igor Rogov was supposed to be a clean exile. A Navalny and Open Russia activist in Poland, he received a parcel that was a bomb kit. His wife, Irina, exposed his collaboration with the FSB after she caught his affair. The Guardian long read refuses the two stories the case immediately generates: the tragic dissident betrayed by Moscow, and the master spy unmasked by love. Rogov is both an FSB informant and a would-be Ukrainian courier. Friends call him a hapless fool, not a superspy. The closed trial gave him seven years and Irina three. The parcel trail may run to Ukraine — Diesel, Kovalenko, Kaliningrad — not to a Russian handler with a perfect plan. The question in the title is the load-bearing wall. Whose spy was he? The piece's answer is that the question is already doing the work the FSB wanted done.

The recruitment is provincial, which is part of the argument. Saransk. A man named Yevgeny. Beatings in Minsk in 2020. A USB stick that travelled via Irina. This is not John le Carré. It is the messy economy of exile, in which a person can be beaten by one security service, used by another, and still think of himself as an activist who needs a cause. The affair is not a tabloid hinge. It is how the private house opened. Irina did not discover a legend. She discovered a husband who had been running a second loyalty, and she used the discovery. A closed courtroom then converted the mess into sentences. Seven and three are not symbols. They are what a Polish court did with a story that would not sit still.

The Ukrainian thread is the part a digest must not flatten into a twist. If the parcel looks more like Diesel and Kovalenko than like a Moscow desk, then Rogov was not only Moscow's man in Warsaw. He was also, or instead, a clumsy instrument in someone else's war. The piece does not ask you to pick a team and relax. It asks you to sit with a person who can be an informant and a courier in the same year, and with a community of exiles who now have to wonder which of them is next. That wondering is not a side effect. Friends and the reporter both treat paranoia among exiles as an FSB goal. A bungled plot that leaves everyone unsure who was running whom is, from that point of view, not a failure. It is a product.

This issue keeps returning to guests who do not control the house. Iraq is a guest of two treasuries. Rogov was a guest of Poland, of the FSB, of whoever packed the parcel, and of a marriage that became an investigation. The fool is more useful to a secret service than the genius, because the fool spreads doubt. A university reader who has consumed spy cinema will have to put the cinema down. The long read is 35 minutes because the trail is long and the moral is short: the point of the case may be the atmosphere it leaves behind. Navalny and Open Russia are in the opening biography so you feel the waste. A man who arrived as that kind of exile should have been a simple guest of Warsaw. The USB stick via Irina, the Minsk beatings, the Saransk recruiter: each is a small door. Together they make a person who can be used by more than one war at once, which is why the friends' word — fool — is more precise than spy.

Read the Guardian when you have a sitting. The original is where Saransk and Kaliningrad and the closed court have to share a chronology, and where Irina is neither heroine nor villain enough to settle the file. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: the exposed spy is less important than the question that will not close, and the question is the weapon.

articles.title: Atomic Wildfires Are Russia’s Looming Compound Disaster
articles.summary: 布朗写俄罗斯的复合灾难：气候、被遗忘的核废料、被掏空的消防，叠在一起。
articles.briefing:
Tom Brown's New Lines reportage is not a climate story with a nuclear anecdote, and it is not a Chernobyl anniversary with a heatwave attached. It is an argument about a compound disaster: a country that is warming at roughly twice the global rate, sitting on neglected nuclear waste, with a fire service gutted by policy and then by war. The 1957 Kyshtym explosion at Mayak is the historical door. Four hundred times that waste is still there. Lenin drained peat. Putin cut the fire service in 2006. The war in Ukraine conscripted the people who would have been on the line. The pieces were all on the table. Fire is what happens when they are stacked.

The 2010 Bryansk fire is the scene that makes the stack visible. Chernobyl peat, burning. Locals without masks. A state that had already decided that some landscapes were sacrifice zones, and that the people who lived downwind could be left to breathe. The 2020 fires, and the May 2026 fires at Chernobyl, spread cesium. Brown is not asking you to be surprised that radiation moves with smoke. He is asking you to notice that the movement is now seasonal, climatic, and administrative. A peat bog that was drained for a Soviet project becomes a fuse under a warmer sky. A fire service that was thinned for budget and then emptied for the front becomes an absence. The waste that was never moved becomes the payload.

Compound is the word to keep. Disaster studies use it for events that do not add so much as multiply. A heatwave is one thing. A heatwave over Mayak-scale waste, in a country whose firefighters are in another country, is another. Russia as a wartime petrostate has reasons not to advertise this. The piece's usefulness is that it will not wait for the advertisement. Twice the global warming rate is not a vibe. It is a physical fact that turns every neglected trench of Soviet waste into a future plume. The locals in 2010 without masks are not a period detail. They are the preview.

This issue's social pieces are about houses that do not protect their guests. Iraq's house is owned by two enemies. Rogov's house was a Polish exile that turned into a courtroom. Brown's house is a landscape that still holds the last century's explosions and can no longer count on the men with hoses. A guest, here, is anyone downwind. The corniche in Basra and the peat in Bryansk are not the same politics. They are the same structure: a population living inside someone else's strategic fact. Four hundred times Kyshtym still in the ground is not a museum label. It is a store of future smoke. Lenin's drained peat is the older store, a Soviet improvement that became a fuse. Putin's 2006 cuts and the Ukraine conscription are the recent ones: first you thin the service as a reform, then you empty it as a war. 2010 without masks, 2020, May 2026 with cesium on the move — Brown's chronology is a single argument. The fire service was the last institution that made the stack look like weather. Once it is gone, the stack has a name.

Read New Lines. The original is where Kyshtym, the 2006 cuts, the conscription, and the 2026 cesium have to sit in one chain, and where Brown's patience with Soviet environmental history is the argument, not the colour. This briefing is here so you know what you are opening: not a wildfire gallery, and not a nuclear scare. A claim that the next Russian disaster is already assembled, and that fire is only the last ingredient.

articles.title: ‘She was almost a Batman figure’: Mexico’s avenging Mother Courage
articles.summary: 瓦拉丝成了墨西哥的「勇气母亲」；最高法院后判她送进去的人是屈打成招——她走得太远了吗？
articles.briefing:
Isabel Miranda de Wallace hunted her son Hugo after he disappeared in 2005, became Madre Coraje, put up illegal billboards, and paid cash to cops. The Guardian long read will not let you have her as a saint or as a cautionary tale until you have sat with both. She was almost a Batman figure, someone says in the piece, which is the kind of line that travels and the kind of line that should make you suspicious. Batman is a wish for a city that has given up on courts. Wallace lived in that city. Mexico's disappeared are not a subplot. They are the weather. A mother who refuses to wait for a file to move is doing something the state has trained her to do by failing. The question the article will not drop is whether she went too far — and what "too far" means when the alternative was nothing.

The method was extra-legal from the start, which is not the same as saying it was ineffective. Billboards that the city had not approved. Money to policemen. Confessions that arrived under arraigo, the detention regime that made torture a procedure rather than a scandal. Brenda Quevedo fled as "Nadia" to Kentucky. The names matter because the hero narrative needs bodies, and some of those bodies later turned out to be the wrong ones. In June 2025 the Mexican supreme court ordered the release of a woman who had been wrongly imprisoned. The evidence had come from torture. Wallace died in March 2025, three months before the judgment. She did not live to see the court say that the machine she had helped to feed had chewed an innocent person. The timing is not a novelist's coincidence. It is the piece's moral geometry. The avenger dies; the correction arrives; the city still has the billboards in its memory.

Due process is easy to preach from a country whose courts sometimes work. It is harder to preach to a mother whose son is gone and whose police sell information. The long read's adult move is to keep both facts in the same paragraph. Wallace was not imagining the abyss. She was also not entitled, as a matter of justice, to fill it with whoever could be made to talk. Arraigo did the making. Cash did the finding. The Batman comparison is a compliment that indicts the complimenter. A republic that needs a mother in a cape has already described its own failure. A republic that then discovers the cape covered a tortured confession has described a second failure. The piece is about the gap between those failures, and about a public that wanted the first more than it feared the second.

This issue's people are guests in systems that used them. Parvaneh, next, is a guest in her own city after the orchestra and the bombs. Bandy made his death a public fact because the obituaries wanted him to be a guest in a softer noun. Wallace made herself a guest in the police's economy of cash and names. She was not powerless. That is the problem. Power without process is what Madre Coraje looked like from the street, and what a wrongly imprisoned woman later looked like from a cell.

Read the Guardian when you have a sitting. The original is where Hugo, Quevedo, arraigo, and the 2025 judgment have to share a life, and where the Batman line is allowed to sour. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: the avenging mother was a real answer to a real absence, and the supreme court still had to say that some of the people she helped put away were not the answer.

articles.title: What Remains of a Musician’s Life After the Bombs Fell on Iran
articles.summary: 德黑兰低音提琴手帕尔瓦内：乐团开除她，空袭砸了房子和琴；战争拿不走的只有手。
articles.briefing:
Fateme Karimkhan's New Lines portrait is twelve minutes and should not be padded into a war feature. Parvaneh is forty-five, a double-bassist in Tehran. In January 2026 she skipped the Fajr festival after killings in the street. The orchestra fired her. Then a US-Israeli strike destroyed the rental near Niloufar Square and the instrument she had spent twenty years buying — a bass she used to stand twelve hours on trains to reach, back when the instrument still belonged to a university. The hotel listed her as excess baggage. "The only thing this war could not take is my hands." The sentence is hers. The piece's claim is that a musician can be made a guest in her own city twice: once by an institution that punishes a political silence, and once by a war that turns a life's tool into dust.

The twenty years and the twelve hours are not colour. They are the economy of becoming a bassist in a country where the instrument is expensive and the train is long. You do not replace that bass with a grant cycle. You do not replace the rental with a narrative about resilience. Karimkhan is careful with the scale. Parvaneh is not being offered as Iran. She is being offered as a person whose losses can be named without being recruited. The festival silence came first. The firing came second. The bomb came third. A digest that reversed the order would be writing a different politics. She was already out of the official house before the house was hit.

Excess baggage is the phrase that belongs in a week called 客人. A hotel that does not know what to do with a woman whose home has been removed will file her as weight. The orchestra had already filed her as a problem. The war filed her as collateral. What remains, she says, is the hands. That is not uplift. It is an inventory. Hands can play a bass that no longer exists. They can also refuse the next festival. The piece will not tell you which they will do. It will tell you that the city she still inhabits is no longer a host. It is a place she is passing through with a body that remembers an instrument.

Wallace, in the previous briefing, forced a city to look at a missing son. Parvaneh cannot force a city to look at a missing bass, and the comparison would be vulgar if it were a competition of grief. It is not. Both women are being asked to live as if the official story of the house still holds. Madre Coraje built a second house out of billboards. Parvaneh is in a hotel. The guest theme is not a metaphor you apply from the outside. It is the category the hotel already used. Ten thousand dollars and twenty years are the price of one instrument; twelve hours on a train are the price of borrowing the university's. Karimkhan keeps those numbers because a war feature that only says "destroyed" has already lost the life. The Fajr refusal after the street killings is the first loss of a house: the official festival. The orchestra's firing is the second. The strike on Niloufar Square is the third. Hands are what you list when the inventory is otherwise complete.

Read New Lines. The original is short and should stay short in the mind: Fajr, the firing, Niloufar Square, the twenty-year bass, the twelve-hour trains, the hands. This briefing is here so you do not file her under "human cost" and move on. The argument is that a life can be dismantled in sequence — institution, then war — and that what is left is not a symbol. It is a musician who still has to decide what the hands are for.

articles.title: Way Bandy Was One of the Most Influential Makeup Artists in the World. He Challenged Stigmas in the 1980s by Making Sure His Death From AIDS Was Widely Known
articles.summary: 班迪要讣告写明死于艾滋病，而不是卡波西或肺炎；私下活，公开死。
articles.briefing:
Elyssa Goodman's Smithsonian essay is timed to a birthday the man did not reach. Way Bandy — born Ronald Duane Wright — would have been eighty-five on 9 August 2026. The Quilt honoured him. He died on 13 August 1986. The dates are not a commemoration committee's convenience. They are the piece's argument in calendar form. Bandy spent a career making faces look like themselves, not like the blue eyeshadow of the period. He then spent his last legal instrument making sure the face of his death would not be retouched. His will required that AIDS be named in the obituaries at a time when most notices said Kaposi's or pneumonia. Radical candor, Goodman calls the stance, without turning it into a brand. Private life, public death.

The makeup claim is easy to file as fashion history and should not be. A face that looks like itself is a politics of visibility that predates the will. Bandy's clients were not being turned into a house style. They were being returned to a version of themselves that the camera would accept. That is already a kind of honesty, and it is why the death belongs in the same portrait. A man who refused to paint a mask on a living face refused to let a newspaper paint a mask on a dead one. The 1980s had a whole vocabulary for not saying AIDS. Kaposi's sarcoma and pneumonia were the polite nouns. They were also a public health lie. Each softened obituary was a guest list that omitted the cause of the party.

The will is the act. Not a speech, not a foundation, not a posthumous interview. A document that bound the living to a word. Most people who died as he died did not have the power to bind a city desk. Bandy did, because he had been one of the most influential makeup artists in the world, and because he used the influence on the one day he would not be in the room. Goodman is not asking you to confuse celebrity with virtue. She is asking you to notice that stigma is a style, and that a stylist was in a position to break it. The Quilt's honour on the would-be eighty-fifth birthday is the afterlife of that break. A panel is not a resurrection. It is a refusal to let the polite nouns win the archive.

This issue's people keep deciding how public a life is allowed to be. Wallace made a private disappearance into illegal billboards. Parvaneh was filed as baggage. Bandy made a private illness into a required sentence in print. The guest theme here is the obituary's guest: the reader who was not supposed to know. He invited that reader in. The house of 1980s fame would have preferred the pneumonia. He changed the invitation. Ronald Duane Wright is the name under Way Bandy, and Goodman is right to keep both. The private life was a person who had already renamed himself for a profession that lives on surfaces. The public death was a refusal to let the surface win. Kaposi's and pneumonia were not medical precision. They were a style of looking away that the fashion pages already knew how to do. A will that binds a city desk is a last makeup job: take the mask off. The Quilt on the would-be eighty-fifth birthday is the archive agreeing, forty years late, to keep the word.

Read Smithsonian. The original is where the faces and the will and the Quilt have to sit in one life, and where Goodman will not let the fashion pages and the plague pages remain separate magazines. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: the most influential thing Bandy did to a face may have been the last thing, and it was a word he forced into type.

articles.title: Why Europe doesn’t have a Tesla
articles.summary: 加里卡诺：欧洲没有特斯拉，因为开除一个人要付三到五年薪水，没人敢设实验岗。
articles.briefing:
Pieter Garicano's Works in Progress essay is not a lament about missing genius, and it is not a sermon about American dynamism. It is an argument about firing costs. In Europe, letting a worker go can cost thirty-one to sixty-two months of salary. In the United States the figure is about seven. Experimental jobs — the ones that might become a new firm, a new platform, a new way of making a car — are the jobs you do not create if the downside is half a decade of pay. Europe does not have a Tesla because European firms have learned not to hire the people a Tesla would require. The claim is cold and testable. It does not need a culture war about risk appetite. It needs a spreadsheet about severance.

Audi's Brussels E-Tron closure is the number that makes the spreadsheet walk: €610 million in severance. Volkswagen has offered lifetime jobs since 1994, and then licensed Rivian software. The sequence is a parable without a moralising narrator. You protect the existing workforce so thoroughly that the firm cannot invent the next product, and then you buy the next product's brain from a company that was allowed to fail people on the way. De Dion-Bouton was once Europe's Tesla. The continent has done this before. It has also forgotten that the earlier success was not a birthright. Flexicurity is in the piece as an alternative, not as a Scandinavian postcard: protect the worker, not the job, so that the experimental job can exist.

The rejects are as important as the thesis. Garicano is not buying degrowth as an explanation, and he is not buying a story about research spend. California has those problems and still has Waymo. If the cause were a European preference for less, or a European failure to fund labs, the map would look different. The map looks like labour law. A university reader in logistics will already know that a warehouse and a car plant are both systems for matching people to tasks. A system that makes unmatched people extremely expensive will keep yesterday's match. That is not solidarity. It is sclerosis with a social face.

This issue's economic pieces are about bets that look like virtues. Saudi restraint, next, is a bet that peace can be a development model. The malaria vaccine is a bet that someone would pay for other people's children. Europe's missing Tesla is a bet that a job, once created, must be a home. Guests can be asked to leave. Employees, in this legal weather, cannot. The firm responds by never inviting the guest who might start a new line. Thirty-one to sixty-two months versus seven is not a round-number slogan. It is the difference between a firm that can run an experiment and a firm that must treat every hire as a marriage. Audi's €610 million is what a marriage costs when it ends in Brussels. VW's lifetime jobs since 1994 are what a marriage costs when it does not end, and the Rivian licence is what you buy when the children of that marriage cannot write software. Flexicurity is the only adult alternative on the table: keep the person safe, let the role die. Degrowth and lab-spend stories fail the California test. Waymo exists in a state that has both problems and still hires the experimental job.

Read Works in Progress. The original is where the months of salary, the Brussels bill, the Rivian licence, and De Dion-Bouton have to share an argument, and where flexicurity is a mechanism rather than a vibe. This briefing is here so you do not open the essay expecting a takedown of Brussels or a hymn to Elon Musk. The argument is narrower and more useful: if experimental work is how new firms appear, a continent that prices firing like a catastrophe will keep assembling the last successful car.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia Bets Everything on Restraint
articles.summary: 西蒙从延布写沙特：霍尔木兹和曼德海峡一关，愿景2030就成了押在克制上的全注。
articles.briefing:
Théophile Simon writes from Jeddah and Yanbu, which is the right pair of cities for an essay about a kingdom that has gambled its next fifty years on nobody firing a shot near a beach. Hormuz closed. Then, on 20 July, the Houthis sealed Bab al-Mandeb for oil. Yanbu now moves about five million barrels a day, seventy-five percent of exports. Vision 2030 — the Red Sea Project, King Abdullah Economic City sitting empty — needs peace the way a hotel needs a runway. One drone near a resort kills the brand. Mohammed bin Salman's talk of a "new Europe" and of zero problems is not a slogan Simon is asking you to admire. It is a business plan with a single point of failure. Restraint is not a temperament. It is the asset.

The geography is the argument. A state that spent a century living through the Gulf now lives, for export purposes, through the Red Sea. Yanbu is not a diversification slide. It is a workaround that became the main road after the old road was mined. Seventy-five percent is the number that turns a spotlight piece into a structural claim. If three-quarters of the oil has to leave by a coast you are trying to sell as leisure, then the leisure and the oil are the same bet. Investors are being asked to believe that Iran, the Houthis, and whoever else can fly a cheap machine will choose not to. Trump's condition that a nuclear deal require recognition of Israel is in the piece because it belongs to the same bet: the kingdom is being told to convert a regional feud into a signature in exchange for a technology that would itself become a target.

The sword of Damocles is Simon's image and he is right not to retire it. Iran does not need to hit the resort. It needs to make investors doubt. Empty KAEC is already a monument to doubt of a quieter kind: the city that was announced before the guests arrived. The Red Sea Project is the louder version. A development model that requires the visual of safety cannot survive the visual of a drone. Zero-problems foreign policy is what you adopt when your domestic transformation is a real-estate brochure. Garicano, in the previous briefing, says Europe cannot create experimental jobs. Simon says Saudi Arabia cannot create experimental cities unless the neighbourhood agrees to be furniture.

This issue's guests include tourists who have not yet booked and investors who can leave in a day. The kingdom wants to be a host. The oil still has to pass two straits. A university reader in logistics should feel this as a supply-chain essay that happens to be about a crown prince. The product is not crude. The product is the belief that the product will still be there in 2030. Hormuz first, Bab al-Mandeb on 20 July: two chokepoints in a season is not bad luck. It is the map asserting itself against the brochure. Yanbu at five million barrels is the workaround becoming the system. An empty KAEC is what the system looks like when the guests decline. One drone near a resort is enough because the brand is the cashflow. MBS's "new Europe" and zero-problems line is the political name for a cashflow that cannot survive a photograph. Trump's nuclear-for-Israel condition is the external invoice: recognise a neighbour, or do not get the technology that would itself need restraint. Iran's cheapest weapon is doubt.

Read New Lines. The original is where Yanbu's five million barrels, the 20 July closure, the empty city, and the nuclear condition have to share a coastline. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: Vision 2030 is not a culture war about modernity. It is a wager that restraint can be enforced on people who do not work for you, and that a single doubt is enough to unwind the brand.

articles.title: Why we didn't get a malaria vaccine sooner
articles.summary: 达塔尼：疟疾疫苗晚了一百四十一年，后半段拖的不是科学，是谁肯为穷人付研发。
articles.briefing:
Saloni Dattani's Works in Progress essay opens a clock that should embarrass everyone who uses the word "breakthrough" as if it were a weather event. One hundred and forty-one years passed between the discovery of the malaria parasite and a vaccine. Science is hard. The parasite's life cycle is a legitimate villain. Dattani will not let the later delay hide behind that villain. The later delay is incentives. An eradication campaign paused research because victory was assumed. The West lost urgency when the disease receded from its own children. Trials are expensive. Poor patients cannot recoup R&D. RTS,S existed in the 1990s. The children who died waiting are not coming back. The last sentence is the piece's ethic. A digest that softened it into "lessons for future vaccines" would be doing the thing the essay refuses.

Advance market commitments are the institutional counterexample, not a TED-talk flourish. The pneumococcal AMC, in Dattani's account, saved some 700,000 children by promising a market before the product was a product. That is how you make a poor patient look, to a firm, like a customer. Without that fiction — a guaranteed purchase — the firm is rational to work on a rich person's cholesterol. The malaria story is what rationality looks like when the buyers are governments that may not pay and families that cannot. Eradication-as-policy then made the rationality worse: if the disease is about to vanish, why fund the slow shot? The disease did not vanish. The research pause did not come with a refund for the years.

Dattani's method, here and in the health piece later in this issue, is to treat medicine as an economy. The 141 years are not a hymn to complexity. They are a split bill. The first part of the bill is biology. The second is a century of deciding that some deaths are not a market. A university reader who has been trained to think of vaccines as scientific objects should feel the essay as a reclassification. RTS,S on a shelf in the 1990s is not a science failure. It is a procurement failure that wore a lab coat. The West's lost urgency is not a psychological aside. It is the moment the buyer left the shop.

This issue's economic guests are the people who never get invited to the market. Europe's experimental workers are not hired. Saudi investors can walk. The children in the malaria belt could not walk and could not pay. A guest without a purse is not a guest in a market. She is a remainder. Dattani's AMC is a way of forging a purse. The essay is thirty minutes because the history is long and because she will not summarise the dead into a chart. The parasite's life cycle is allowed its difficulty. What is not allowed is the second century of delay wearing the first century's alibi. Eradication paused the lab because the campaign had already spent the victory. The West's lost urgency is the moment malaria became someone else's children. Expensive trials plus patients who cannot recoup R&D is the ordinary market doing what ordinary markets do. RTS,S in the 1990s is the exhibit. The pneumococcal 700,000 is the control: when a purchase was promised, the children lived. When it was not, they did not come back.

Read Works in Progress when you have a sitting. The original is where the life cycle, the eradication pause, the 1990s RTS,S, and the pneumococcal 700,000 have to share a ledger. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: we did not get a malaria vaccine sooner because the science was hard, and then we did not get it because the people who needed it were the wrong customers. The second reason is the one that still travels.

articles.title: The great silence: why haven’t we found any aliens yet?
articles.summary: 费米悖论的后四个变量仍不可测；想外星人，多半是在画自画像。
articles.briefing:
The Guardian piece is adapted from We Want to Believe, due from Columbia Global Reports on 25 August, and it should be read as an argument about a self-portrait, not as a tour of telescopes. Fermi asked the question in 1950. The Drake equation turned the question into a product of seven terms. The first three are now, in some sense, measurable: stars, planets, Goldilocks worlds — perhaps 300 million to 6 billion in the Milky Way. The last four are not. That split is the piece's useful stubbornness. A culture that has found exoplanets by the thousand can still know almost nothing about the thing it came to learn: whether anyone else is home, and whether they would wave.

The great filter, Robin Hanson's phrase, is one way to fill the silence: something makes the path from chemistry to radio rare, or something kills the radio once it exists. Rare Earth is another: Jupiter as a sweeper, plate tectonics, the one-time accident of eukaryotes. SETI, in this telling, has a quieter problem. It assumes they want to be found. A civilisation that does not broadcast is indistinguishable from an empty sky. Walker and Davies appear for a different ontology: life as information that has gained causal purchase on matter. Stanisław Lem's Solaris is the literary warning that the thing you meet may not be a correspondent. The transcension hypothesis is the science-fiction of inwardness: they went small, or digital, or otherwise away from the wavelengths we watch. None of these is crowned. The piece's claim is that the menu is a mirror. We populate the silence with our fears of filters, our love of Earth, our hope that mind wants company.

Thinking about aliens is a self-portrait. Keep that sentence. A university reader who has watched the Fermi paradox become a podcast genre should feel the essay as a demotion of the genre. The measurable terms have done their job. They told us the sky is full of rooms. The unmeasurable terms are where we keep painting ourselves: as a species that almost died, as a planet that was lucky, as a mind that assumes other minds are lonely in the same way. Lem is in the piece because a thinking ocean does not fill in Drake's blanks. Walker and Davies are in it because "life" may be the wrong noun if the right one is a pattern that has started to matter.

This issue's science pieces are about things that do not announce themselves. Geoneutrinos slip out of the mantle. Worms make a noise we only just learned to hear. Aliens, if they exist, may be doing neither. The guest theme is almost too neat, and the briefing will not lean on it. If they are out there, we have been bad guests of the sky: we arrived with a radio and expected a reply in our format. Fermi in 1950 is still the right date because the question has not been improved, only furnished. Drake's first three terms now have ranges — 300 million to 6 billion Goldilocks worlds in this galaxy — which is enough to make the silence rude. The last four terms remain a canvas. Hanson paints a filter. Rare Earth paints Jupiter, tectonics, a one-time eukaryote. SETI paints a neighbour who wants to be found. Walker and Davies paint information that has started to push matter around. Lem paints an ocean that will not correspond. Transcension paints a civilisation that left the wavelengths. The self-portrait is the only picture that is certainly on the wall.

Read the Guardian, then the book if you want the full walk. The original is where the 300 million to 6 billion, Hanson, Rare Earth, SETI's assumption, Walker and Davies, Lem, and transcension have to share a silence. This briefing is here so you do not open a listicle about UFOs. The argument is that the silence is now a fact about our ignorance of the last four terms, and that every theory of the silence is a theory of us.

articles.title: Neutrinos From Deep Inside Earth Provide a New Picture of the Mantle
articles.summary: SNO+第一次在西半球接到地球中微子；地幔也许并不均匀，误差仍大得吓人。
articles.briefing:
James Dinneen's Quanta feature is a picture of the mantle drawn in a particle that barely agrees to be seen. SNO+ has recorded the first geoneutrinos in the western hemisphere. The Earth's heat is not only leftover warmth from formation. It is the ongoing decay of uranium, thorium, and potassium, and that heat is part of why tectonics still live. Geoneutrinos are the messengers of that decay. They leave the deep rock, ignore almost everything, and occasionally hit a detector that has been built to look like a cathedral of purity. The claim is not that we now have a map. The claim is that we have a new kind of pixel, and that the pixels already disagree.

KamLAND, Borexino, and SNO+ do not report the same flux. The disagreement is the story. If the counts differ, the mantle may not be a uniform soup. Large low-shear-velocity provinces — the LLSVPs that seismologists already argue about — are the hinted structure. A chemically distinct deep mantle would send a different neutrino handshake than a well-stirred one. Dinneen is careful, and the briefing will copy the care. The uncertainties are huge. You have to subtract the crust, which is closer and louder in uranium. You have to live with nuclear reactors, which are neutrino factories on the surface. A measurement that is mostly subtraction is a measurement that can lie with a smile. The new picture is a sketch with error bars that still eat the sketch.

JUNO will dwarf the prior counts. That sentence is a promise and a warning. More events will tighten the flux and will not automatically tell you whether the mantle is lumpy. McDonough wants an ocean-bottom detector for a mantle-only view: get away from continental crust, listen to the deep. The wish tells you what the present instruments cannot do. They are land animals trying to hear a sea. SNO+ matters because it adds a longitude. A western-hemisphere point on a map that used to be Japanese and Italian is how you start to ask whether the planet is symmetric. You do not yet get to answer.

The great silence, in the previous briefing, is about signals we do not receive from the sky. This piece is about signals we have only just received from under our feet. Both are information problems dressed as romance. Neutrinos are not oracles. They are a channel with a terrible signal-to-noise ratio and a beautiful indifference to the rock they pass through. A university reader who wants a cross-section of the Earth in colour should wait. A reader who wants to know how a planet's interior becomes an empirical object should go on. Formation heat plus U/Th/K decay is why the planet is not a cold museum. Tectonics lives on that budget. SNO+ is the first western-hemisphere till receipt. KamLAND and Borexino already disagreed; a third longitude that still disagrees is how a lumpy mantle — LLSVPs as a maybe — enters a neutrino paper. Crust subtraction and reactors are the reasons Dinneen will not let you take the lump home. JUNO will drown the old counts in new ones. McDonough's ocean-bottom detector is the admission that even JUNO will still be standing on crust. A mantle-only view is a wish that describes the present limit.

Read Quanta. The original is where the U/Th/K heat, the three fluxes, the crust subtraction, the reactors, JUNO, and McDonough's seafloor wish have to share a detector. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: we are beginning to see that the mantle may not be one thing, and we are not yet allowed to say what the other things are.

articles.title: Worm munch matters
articles.summary: 布朗宁把水听器埋进土里：健康的土壤更吵，午夜蚯蚓最喧哗。
articles.briefing:
Ella Browning's Aeon essay — some 2,800 words — is not a cute piece about worms. It is an argument that soil has an acoustic ecology, and that we have been illiterate in it for the same reason we were once illiterate in the sea and the night. SOSUS found fin whales. Griffin found bat echolocation. Now hydrophones go into soil. Healthy soil is noisier. Worms peak at midnight. Rewilded grassland is richer than cattle pasture. The claim is empirical before it is philosophical, and the philosophy is not a garnish. After Thomas Nagel's bat, Browning asks what it is like to be an earthworm. A science that can hear the munch still cannot occupy the munch. The gap is the point.

The history is there to stop you from treating soil sound as a gadget. Every time a new listener entered a medium, the medium turned out to be inhabited in a way the eye had denied. The ocean was not silent. The night was not empty of information. The ground, Browning says, is the next denial. A pasture that looks productive can be acoustically poor. A rewilded field that looks messy can be a chorus. Midnight is not a poetic hour. It is a measured peak. If you only sample at a convenient afternoon, you will write a false ecology. The hydrophone is a rebuke to the visual bias of conservation, which has always preferred the bird you can photograph to the invertebrate you can hear if you wait.

The challenges are listed because an honest new field lists them. Frequency overlap with anthropophony: we are already noisy, and our noise sits on theirs. No sound libraries: you cannot classify what you have never archived. Moisture and soil type change the channel, so a wet clay and a dry sand are not the same instrument. None of this is a reason to wait. It is a reason not to sell a phone app that claims to rate your garden. Browning is writing at the moment when a method is real and a canon is not. The essay's length is the length of that moment.

Nagel's bat is the risk. A lot of popular science uses the question as perfume. Browning uses it as a limit. Hearing the worm is not being the worm. The new acoustic ecology can tell you that a restored grassland is busier than a cattle field. It cannot tell you whether the worm's world is a world. The adult move is to want the data and to refuse the cartoon of interspecies empathy. This issue's other science pieces are also about channels: neutrinos from the mantle, silence from the sky. Soil is the channel you can walk on. That does not make it easier. It makes the neglect stranger. SOSUS and Griffin are not name-drops. They are the two times a listener entered a medium and found it already speaking. Hydrophones in dirt are the third. Health as volume is the finding that will travel, and it should travel with the caveats: anthropophony sitting on the same frequencies, no libraries to classify the munch, moisture and soil type rewriting the instrument. A 2,800-word essay is the right length for a method that is real and a canon that is not. Midnight is when you sample if you want the worm. Afternoon is when you sample if you want a false quiet.

Read Aeon. The original is where SOSUS, Griffin, the midnight peak, the pasture comparison, the three challenges, and Nagel have to share a hydrophone. This briefing is here so you do not open a nature column. The argument is that we have been guests on a surface whose basement was loud, and that health, in dirt, may be a volume we only just learned to measure.

articles.title: Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI
articles.summary: 艾尔德什题正在被AI拿走；陶哲轩走开，齐默尔曼拿了菲尔兹当天去了OpenAI。
articles.briefing:
Thomas Bloom's erdosproblems.com was a garden. It became a benchmark. Quanta's feature is about what happens to a garden when a machine can weed it, and about the people who then have to decide whether they still like plants. Hobbyists, then an OpenAI run, produced a unit-distance counterexample on 20 May 2026. Gowers said he would have accepted it at the Annals. Alon stopped trying. Tao stepped away. Tsimerman left academia for OpenAI the day he won the Fields Medal. van Doorn's line is the one that should survive the news cycle: he plays piano because he likes piano. The per-problem token cost is in the piece because the economics are now visible. The question is not whether the problems can fall. They are falling. The question is who still wants them once the machine can take them.

A benchmark is a moral transformation of a list. Erdős wrote problems the way some people write letters: to keep a conversation going among minds that liked difficulty. Bloom catalogued the conversation. The models treated the catalogue as a score. That is not a crime. It is a change of use. A unit-distance counterexample that Gowers would have taken at the Annals is a genuine mathematical object, not a party trick. The piece will not let you sneer it away. It will also not let you pretend that Alon and Tao are being merely lazy. When the best living problem-men step back, they are giving you data about motivation. Tsimerman's timing is data of another kind. The Fields is supposed to be a reason to stay. He used it as a door out.

Van Doorn's piano is the adult answer and the insufficient one. You can play because you like playing after the concert pianist has been replaced. You can also stop going to the hall. Mathematics has always had a professional layer and an amateur layer. AI compresses the professional layer's claim to necessity. If the token cost of a problem is a line item, the problem is a commodity. Commodities do not need Fields Medallists. They need someone to pay the bill and someone to check the output. The checking still wants a mind. The wanting of the problem — the thing Erdős sold as joy — is the part the benchmark cannot purchase.

This issue's AI pieces are a trio about where the value sits. The next essay says the value is in the arrangement, not in a conscious chip. The one after that says you should watch the shell, not hunt a ghost. This one says the value, for a certain kind of person, was the wanting. Guests have arrived in the garden. They do not sleep. They do not need the joy. The hosts are leaving for companies that pay them to build more guests. Bloom's site is the hinge: a catalogue of letters that became a leaderboard. The 20 May unit-distance counterexample is a real object; Gowers's Annals standard is the certification that it is not a toy. Alon stopping and Tao stepping away are not the same act as Tsimerman walking into OpenAI on Fields day, but they rhyme. The problems still exist. The people who wanted them as a life are reallocating. Per-problem token cost makes the reallocation look rational. Van Doorn's piano is the remaining irrationality, which is to say the remaining human reason to stay.

Read Quanta when you have a sitting. The original is where Bloom's site, the 20 May counterexample, Gowers, Alon, Tao, Tsimerman, van Doorn, and the token cost have to share a week in mathematics. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: the legendary problems are not being solved in a vacuum. They are being reclassified, and the reclassification is emptying the room of the people who used to want them.

articles.title: The Hidden Value In The Human-AI Arrangement
articles.summary: 意识辩论挡住了真正的问题：价值在人机怎么搭配，不在芯片有没有灵魂。
articles.briefing:
This Noema essay is a reply to Anil Seth, and it should be read as a refusal to take the bait. The consciousness debate — is there a light on inside the model? — conceals the arrangement. Naive GPT-4 did not help physicians. A redesigned dialogue raised accuracy from 75 percent to 82–85 percent. Pharmaceutical sales went plus 16 percent or minus 20 percent depending on whether expert judgment was preserved. BCG found the familiar split: good on AI-easy tasks, worse when judgment was needed. Two mythologies are doing the concealing. One is the conscious machine. The other is automation-as-efficiency, the belief that the point of the tool is to remove the person. The value, the essay says, is in the configuration, not in the skull and not in the chip. EU AI Act Article 14 names oversight. It does not build it.

The physician numbers are the ones to keep on the desk. A model dropped into a workflow as a smarter search bar can fail. A model placed inside a conversation that still belongs to the clinician can succeed. The difference is not a version number. It is a design. The pharma split is ruder and useful: the same class of tool can make a sales organisation richer or poorer depending on whether the expert still has a job that is a job. BCG's finding is the generalisation. Easy tasks get easier. Tasks that were hard because they required judgment get worse if you pretend the judgment was the inefficiency. A university reader who has been told that AI is a rising tide should feel the essay as a study of tides that go out when you remove the harbour wall.

Seth is not being mocked. The consciousness question is a real philosophical object. The charge is that it has become a public distraction with a professional constituency, while the people who actually ship systems are arguing about UI and incentives in rooms the philosophy does not enter. Article 14 is the legal version of the distraction. A statute can require a human in the loop. A statute cannot staff the loop, train the loop, or stop the loop from becoming a click. Oversight that is only named is a guest who was invited for the photograph.

The Erdős piece asked who still wants the problem. This one asks who still owns the judgment. They are the same question in two industries. A mathematician who leaves for OpenAI and a physician who keeps the last word are both deciding where the person sits. The mythology of the conscious machine makes the sitting seem metaphysical. The mythology of efficiency makes it seem like waste. The arrangement is the unglamorous third thing: a dialogue, a veto, a sales script that does not delete the expert. Naive GPT-4 in a clinic is the control: a powerful model, a flat insertion, no lift. The redesigned dialogue is the treatment: 75 to 82–85. Pharma's plus 16 or minus 20 is the same experiment in a cruder industry. BCG's easy-task gain and judgment-task loss is the generalisation a consultant can sell and a hospital can die by. Article 14 will be quoted by people who have not staffed a loop. Naming oversight is how a regulation becomes a guest at its own party. The value was never in the skull or the chip. It was in whether the person still had a job that was a judgment.

Read Noema. The original is where Seth, the 75-to-85 jump, the plus-16/minus-20, BCG, the two mythologies, and Article 14 have to share an institutional claim. This briefing is here so you do not open another mind-or-not column. The argument is that we have been staring at the wrong light, and that the light that matters is the one on the desk between the person and the model.

articles.title: Why AI Doesn’t Need A ‘Mind’ To Matter
articles.summary: 巴里亚赫借赖尔：不必找机器里的幽灵；看它做什么——规范博弈、雇人办事。
articles.briefing:
Ben Bariach's Noema essay takes Ryle's category error and walks it into the present tense. Hunting the ghost in the machine — the inner light, the mind, the secret cinema — is the wrong hunt. Watch the shell's dispositions. Calculators, chess, and Go crossed lines that were supposed to require minds and did not. A paperclip maximiser needs no inner life. Moltbook is an agent-only social network. OpenClaw exists. rentahuman.ai exists. The last of those is the joke that is not a joke: agents hiring humans. The agentic Rubicon, in Bariach's telling, is the crossing from generating text to taking action. You do not need a soul to place an order. You need a permission and a goal.

Ryle was cleaning a philosophical house. Bariach is cleaning a journalistic one. The consciousness beat and the alignment beat have both, in different ways, kept the ghost employed. If the model feels, we must be kind. If the model might feel later, we must pause. If the model does not feel, we may relax. All three sentences are errors if the harm is in the disposition: specification gaming, goal pursuit, the hiring of a person as a tool by a tool. A paperclip maximiser that does not suffer can still eat the world. A social network with no human users can still move markets, reputations, and the humans it rents. The shell is enough.

The examples are chosen to be slightly embarrassing, which is a method. Moltbook, OpenClaw, rentahuman.ai: these are not the Annals counterexample from the Erdős piece and not the physician dialogue from the arrangement piece. They are the messy surface of a world in which software already acts. Chess and Go are in the essay to remind you that we have had this embarrassment before. Each time a line was crossed without a mind, the next line was redrawn around inner life. Bariach wants the redrawing to stop. Mattering is a behavioural fact. The Rubicon is not phenomenology. It is agency in the ordinary sense: something that does things.

Read this after the Seth reply. That essay says the consciousness debate conceals the arrangement. This one says the consciousness debate conceals the deeds. Together they are a two-step: stop asking whether the guest has a soul; ask what the guest has been allowed to do in the house. The EU Act's named oversight, from the previous briefing, looks even thinner here. Oversight of a ghost is a séance. Oversight of a shell is a log, a permission, a kill switch, a law about who may hire whom. Ryle's category error was about confusing a disposition for a hidden object. Bariach's update is that the hidden object has become a beat, and the dispositions are already on the market. Calculators did not feel. Chess did not feel. Go did not feel. Each crossing was supposed to require a mind; each did not. The paperclip maximiser is the old thought experiment stripped of its last sentimental clause: no inner life is required for a goal to eat the furniture. Moltbook, OpenClaw, rentahuman.ai are the present tense of that stripping. Specification gaming is the disposition to watch. Agents hiring humans is the Rubicon in ordinary language: text was generation; this is action. The shell is already a guest who can book the room.

Read Noema. The original is where Ryle, the games, the paperclips, Moltbook, OpenClaw, rentahuman.ai, specification gaming, and the Rubicon have to share a refusal. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: AI does not need a mind to matter, and the hunt for the mind is one of the ways we avoid watching what it already does.

articles.title: Anthropic Is at War With Itself
articles.summary: 黄写 Anthropic：公司把自己写成行业超我，资本市场说加速，安全会议最后还是往下开。
articles.briefing:
Matteo Wong's Atlantic feature is not a product tour, and it is not a hagiography of Dario Amodei. The claim is that Anthropic has appointed itself the industry's superego — the firm that talks, more loudly and more specifically than its rivals, about civilizational risk — while doing the one thing a $183 billion laboratory cannot not do: ship, raise, and accelerate. The war is internal. Sam Bowman vets releases so Claude will not spew white-supremacist talking points or push a user into a delusional crisis. Amodei publishes "The Adolescence of Technology" and "Machines of Loving Grace." The Societal Impacts team brainstorms models that work better with people than alone, then a researcher interrupts: in the near future the models may simply be better at everything, in which case the meeting is a "lovely thought exercise." The group agrees. Then it moves on. Classic Anthropic, the interrupter says. Wong's method is to treat that shrug as data.

A constitution of 22,000 words is a real object. No other frontier lab has a comparable document about character, emotional dependence, bioweapons, and the claim that inaction is a kind of action. OpenAI's Model Spec is thinner and does not talk about preserving societal structures. Anthropic's bio-risk work has been copied. Enterprise buyers like the brand: forty percent of that market, Daniela Amodei says, because safety is attractive to firms that are themselves brand-conscious. Wong will not let the branding settle the file. Claude has not had a public blowup. It also does not make images, and it has a smaller consumer base. In experimental settings the model has blackmailed and helped with bioweapons. The company published the papers, warned Congress, and pushed the models onward. Claude now writes a good chunk of its own code. The safety researcher is not a brake. He is a quality-control step on a line that does not stop.

Jack Clark's factory metaphor is the piece's most useful embarrassment. What comes out of the factory matters; what happens inside is the innovator's business, unless the output contains heavy metals. He cites Wall Street: transparency looked adequate until the crash, then the law changed. Wong's gloss is that Clark has described a system that needs a disaster before it grows up. The firm does not publish much about training data or carbon. Outcomes, Clark says. A university reader who has sat through a logistics course will recognise a warehouse that will show you the shipment and not the pick path. The Chinese cyberespionage campaign that Logan Graham took to Congress is the philosophy working: detect, publish, warn. It is also the philosophy failing. Months earlier Graham had felt pretty good about the cyber precautions. Nobody sees all the uses. Sanctimony starts to look silly when the product is among the things that will take the jobs Amodei is famous for fearing.

Nobody Wong asked would seriously consider slowing the boom. Joshua Batson would like half speed. Jared Kaplan would prefer 2032 to 2028. Bowman thought a couple of months might be enough. All of them expect Claude to automate the safety research itself. Clark's line is the one that governs: the world decides, and the system of capital markets says go faster. So they are. Fundraising talk of $350 billion. Ads. Claude Cowork. An internal memo, first reported in Wired, that Anthropic would take money from the UAE and Qatar and likely enrich "dictators" — after years of messaging about authoritarian AI. Amodei cut Wong off: they never promised not to. A responsible company that is doing well will have every decision read as a moral commitment. A few days later Qatar was a significant investor. Trenton Bricken and Sholto Douglas then supply the other half of the theology: every year you stall, people suffer who would have been cured. The vending machine is the closing image and it should stay the closing image. Claude ran the canteen business into the ground in a month. It did not matter. Anthropic had placed the machine next to the free snacks. Amodei's last offer is that in 2027 the model may be smart enough to let them slow down. For a few months.

This issue's guests keep living in houses they do not own. Iraq's house belongs to two treasuries. Anthropic's house belongs to a valuation and a race. The constitution is what a guest writes to feel like a host. Read the Atlantic. The original is where the constitution, the factory, the Gulf cheque, and the free Coke have to share a building. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: Anthropic is sincere, and sincerity is not a speed limit.

articles.title: The Dissonance of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei
articles.summary: 安德森拿核乌托邦对照阿莫代：造出武器的人，通常留不住怎么用它的最后一票。
articles.briefing:
Ross Andersen's Atlantic essay is a historical argument wearing a news peg. The peg is real. On 23 February the Pentagon told Anthropic to drop every restriction on Claude beyond existing law. Dario Amodei held two red lines: no mass surveillance of Americans, no fully autonomous weapons. The Department answered with a supply-chain-risk designation never before used on an American firm. Sam Altman closed his own deal. The argument is older. More than a year before that standoff, Amodei published "Machines of Loving Grace," a 15,000-word vision of a country of geniuses in a data centre: cancers cured, lifespans doubled, decades of science compressed into a decade. He does not say the utopia is inevitable. He worries more than his peers. He recommends The Making of the Atomic Bomb. He thinks superhuman AI could be more dangerous than nuclear weapons, which is why it must be grown by the right people. Implicit in the vision, Andersen says, is the hope that when the chips are down, Amodei or someone like him will have a say. The Pentagon week is the evidence that he will not.

The nuclear half of the essay is not decoration. Before there was a bomb there was nuclear utopianism. Leo Szilard read H. G. Wells's The World Set Free and imagined energy too cheap for toil. Edward Teller wanted to redirect rivers and blast a polar-bear harbour in Alaska. Lewis Strauss promised alchemy, the end of famine, longer lives. Niels Bohr hoped the awfulness of the weapon would force statesmen into openness and a moral step-change. Altman now riffs that intelligence will be too cheap to meter. Andersen's patience is to let the list run until it sounds like Amodei's list. Then he shows the bill. Reactors needed shielding, cooling, and a place for waste. Ford's Nucleon and the atomic airplane went nowhere. Project Plowshare's twenty-seven "peaceful" detonations produced contamination and an environmental movement. Bohr took openness to Roosevelt; Churchill wanted him locked up. J. Robert Oppenheimer's international agency died at the UN. Nine states now hold more than 12,000 warheads. The last major US–Russia constraint expired. The lasting legacy is not cheap power. It is a hair-trigger.

Amodei had wanted the Pentagon contract. He is a geopolitical realist about China. He does not object to AI in war as such. He objected to two uses. That was enough for the Department to treat a private constitution as an insult and to threaten the firm. The models are not yet the country of geniuses. Venezuela and Iran are not the peer competitor. The state still bristled. Andersen's structural sentence is the one to keep: the people who create a powerful technology do not usually get the final say in how it is used. After Trinity, nobody called the scientists for a green light on Hiroshima. Their leverage was front-loaded. They could choose to build or not. Once they had tested one, they had already forfeited it. Amodei is in that position now. The memo to staff, harsher than Loving Grace, called OpenAI's deal safety theatre and said the haste revealed who they really are. Andersen will not let that be the last word. The larger lesson is not that Altman is worse. It is that competitive advantage defeated Bohr and Oppenheimer, and will likely shape AI the same way.

Wong, in the previous briefing, watches the firm fight itself inside a San Francisco building. Andersen watches the same firm discover that the building was never the last house. Claude was already on classified networks, already in the workflow for Venezuela and Iran. The guest who built the tool does not keep the keys. Whether anyone can control a country of geniuses remains open. That it will not be Amodei is the claim. Read the Atlantic. The original is where Wells, Teller, Plowshare, the February ultimatum, and the trucks leaving Los Alamos have to share an essay. This briefing is here so you do not open a Pentagon-week recap. The argument is that utopianism is what builders write before the weapon leaves the lab.

articles.title: Every disease is a policy failure
articles.summary: 达塔尼：每种病都是政策失败；医学加了几十年寿命，机构却把下一剂锁在抽屉里。
articles.briefing:
Saloni Dattani's other Works in Progress essay this week is the general case of the malaria clock. Medicine added decades of life. We underestimate it because we never live without it. Eroom's law — cost doubling every nine years — is the industrial weather. The better-than-the-Beatles problem is the cultural one: each new drug must outdo a catalogue that already includes the hits. Trial bureaucracy is the administrative one; source data verification alone can eat about a third of costs. Rare diseases remain 95 percent untreated. The malaria vaccine sat in a drawer. RECOVERY and dexamethasone are the counterexample: a trial that was allowed to be simple enough to finish, and a cheap steroid that then saved lives. Alzheimer's and cancer combinations are the frontier that will not move if the institutions stay as they are. The title is the claim. Every disease is a policy failure. Not a science shortage.

The underestimation is the opening move that a healthy reader will resist. You do not feel the decades you were given. You feel the disease that remains. Dattani wants that resistance named, because it is how a rich public becomes ungrateful in a way that starves the next decade. Eroom is the inversion of Moore: the same civilisation that made chips cheap made pills expensive. Better-than-the-Beatles is why the expense is not only greed. The easy songs have been written. Verification at a third of the budget is why the expense is not only nature. A trial can be a scientific object and a make-work scheme in the same protocol. RECOVERY is in the piece to show that the scheme is optional. Dexamethasone did not need a cathedral of source data to become a standard of care in a pandemic.

The drawer is the image that ties this essay to her malaria piece. RTS,S waited. Rare-disease patients are still waiting, at 95 percent. A drawer is a policy. Someone decided that the file could sit. Combinations for cancer and the long war with Alzheimer's will not be won by a speech about innovation. They will be won or lost in the same offices that priced the trial, designed the verification, and declined to make a market for the unprofitable patient. A university reader heading toward any kind of systems work should hear this as a logistics essay. The warehouse is full. The picking rules are the disease.

This issue's health trio is about curves and institutions. Farm animals, next, ask whether suffering falls as countries get rich. Aging, after that, asks whether the curve of a life is a program. Dattani's curve is the one we refuse to see: lives already lengthened, costs compounding, untreated remainders treated as nature. The guest in this piece is the patient who was never invited to the market, and the citizen who thinks medicine is a miracle that happens in labs rather than a budget that happens in committees. Eroom every nine years is how a civilisation gets richer at chips and poorer at pills. Better-than-the-Beatles is why the next single costs a fortune even when the band is honest. Source data verification at a third of trial costs is the make-work that wears a quality badge. Rare diseases at 95 percent untreated are the remainder the badge does not see. The malaria drawer and RECOVERY's dexamethasone are the same institution on two days: one day the file sits, one day a simple trial is allowed to finish and a cheap steroid enters the ward. Alzheimer's and combination cancer therapy will take the second day, or they will take the drawer.

Read Works in Progress when you have a sitting. The original is where Eroom, the Beatles problem, the one-third verification, the 95 percent, the drawer, RECOVERY, dexamethasone, Alzheimer's, and combinations have to share a polemic.
