This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: the future of medicine is not waiting for a genius. It is waiting for a polity that treats the remaining diseases as failures it owns.

articles.title: Will farm animals always suffer?
articles.summary: 工厂化养殖跟着收入走；若稳定曲线的另一边存在，全球头数仍会淹没福利进步。
articles.briefing:
Gould and Flynn-Do ask a Kuznets question about pain. Factory farming follows income with an ugly regularity: around a thousand dollars, chickens industrialise; around ten thousand, battery cages; around thirty thousand, pigs go into warehouses. The curve that made child labour fall in rich countries is the hopeful analogy. The curve that made waste keep growing is the other. Which kind of thing is animal suffering? Meat intake plateaus around 150 kilograms in some rich countries. Germany eats less meat and twice as many animals, because the plate shifted toward chicken and fish. Cage-free is cheap to adopt. Cultivated meat is still about ten times the price. New Zealand, Germany, and Sweden offer a glimpse of the other side of the curve. The global headcount still swamps the welfare gains. The title's "always" is not rhetoric. It is a race between a possible decline in suffering per animal and a certain rise in animals.

The income thresholds are the argument's spine. This is not a story about national character. It is a story about what a food system does when a population can pay for muscle that does not walk outside. A logistics student should recognise a series of process upgrades. The chicken is the first because it is small and fast. The cage is the next because it is dense. The warehouse pig is the luxury of a society that can refrigerate a surplus of pork. Kuznets, used honestly, is not a promise that the line will bend. It is a shape some harms take if politics and technology intervene. Child labour bent because it was banned and because capital found other ways to use children, namely schools. Waste did not bend because the other way was more waste. Animals can go either way.

Germany's less-meat, more-animals fact is the one that punishes vegetarian slogans that stop at kilograms. A diet can lose weight and gain lives. Fish and chicken are efficient at turning feed into flesh and efficient at multiplying the number of creatures who pass through the machine. Cage-free is the cheap win, which is why it matters: some suffering is a coordination problem, not a price problem. Cultivated meat at 10× is still a price problem. The glimpse in NZ, Germany, and Sweden is real and small. The global numbers are the swamp. A rich country's reform that is drowned by a poor country's first thousand dollars is not a failure of the rich country. It is the shape of the curve.

Dattani has just told you that remaining human diseases are policy failures. This essay asks whether remaining animal suffering is the same kind of object. Sometimes. Cage-free is a policy. The 10× meat is a technology that has not yet become a policy. The headcount is a demographic fact that no European statute can repeal. The guest theme is uncomfortable and should stay uncomfortable. The animals are not guests. They are inventory. The question is whether a rich world can stop treating them that way without exporting the inventory to the next country that just crossed a thousand dollars. The $1k / $10k / $30k steps are a process map, not a morality play: chickens first, cages next, warehouse pigs when the fridge and the wallet can take them. Meat at a 150 kg plateau is the hopeful bend. Germany eating less and farming twice as many lives is the bend's trick. NZ, Germany, and Sweden are a glimpse, not a destination. Always, in the title, is the race between per-animal welfare and the global headcount. The headcount is winning.

Read Works in Progress. The original is where the $1k/$10k/$30k steps, the 150 kg plateau, Germany's double headcount, cage-free, the 10× cultivated meat, and the NZ–Germany–Sweden glimpse have to share a Kuznets chart. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: suffering may not be eternal, and the global count may still make the decline look like a rounding error.

articles.title: Why Aging May Be a Program, Not a Breakdown
articles.summary: 曹俊岳：衰老不是分子慢慢坏掉，而是「细胞社会」按剧本换台；救援得赶在中年之前。
articles.briefing:
Junyue Cao, at Rockefeller, is interviewed in Quanta, and the Q&A form should not fool you into filing this as a chat. The claim is an argument: aging is an upstream program, not a linear accumulation of molecular damage. Twenty-one million mouse cells, five life stages. The same genomic regions open and close at each stage — some 280,000 of them. A cell society is remodelled on a schedule, the way a tree in autumn is not a summer tree that has broken. It is a tree executing a season. Humans, in the picture Cao wants you to take seriously, age abruptly from the mid-forties to the late fifties. Rescue, if rescue is the word, must start before middle age. After the program has changed the society, you are not repairing a scratch. You are arguing with a new constitution.

The breakdown model is the one a century of biochemistry made intuitive. Errors accumulate. Telomeres shorten. Junk builds up. Death is the sum. Cao's data do not require you to throw the junk out. They require you to notice a choreography that the junk model does not predict: the same regions, the same stages, a remodel that looks like a decision. Twenty-one million cells are a society in the literal sense the metaphor needs. A society can decline because its members wear out. It can also decline because it has voted, in some distributed way, to become a different society. The 280,000 regions are the ballot. Five stages are the election nights. The autumn tree is the image that stops the interview from sounding like a TED transcript. Leaves do not fall because they forgot how to be leaves. They fall because the tree has a season.

The human mid-life jump is the part that will be abused in headlines and should not be abused here. An abrupt remodel from the mid-forties to the late fifties is a claim about timing, not a claim that a forty-three-year-old is young in every tissue. It is a claim about when an intervention would still be speaking to the old constitution. Start later and you are a guest in a house that has already been rebuilt. Dattani's policy failures are about institutions that wait. Cao's program is about a biology that will not wait. The two pieces belong in the same issue because both are arguments against the idea that time is a smooth enemy. Time, here, is staged.

Farm animals, in the previous briefing, suffer on an income schedule. People, in this one, may age on a genomic schedule. Neither schedule is a destiny if you can change the rules. Both are destinies if you keep using the breakdown story: a little more damage, a little more meat, a little more cost, and then surprise. Cao wants the surprise removed. There is an upstream program. The interview is the form. The argument is the content. Twenty-one million mouse cells across five stages are not a metaphor for society. They are the society being counted. Two hundred and eighty thousand regions opening and closing on cue are what a program looks like when you stop staring at single-molecule scars. The autumn tree is there so you do not hear "program" as a conspiracy. A season is a program that does not need a villain. The human jump from the mid-forties to the late fifties is a timing claim: the remodel is not a gentle slope. Rescue before middle age is the practical sentence. After the constitution changes, you are a guest in a house that has already been rebuilt, arguing with last year's keys.

Read Quanta. The original is where the 21 million cells, the five stages, the 280,000 regions, the autumn tree, the mid-forties-to-late-fifties jump, and the before-middle-age rescue have to share a Q&A that is really a brief. This briefing is here so the argument is already in the room: aging may not be what happens when a machine wears down. It may be what a society of cells does on purpose, and the purpose has a clock.
